summary: Defines the Telnet Output Carriage-Return Disposition option, NAOCRD, which negotiates how the receiver handles carriage-return characters in output. The RFC is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: NAOCRD lets Telnet peers negotiate who handles carriage returns in output and what handling to use. RFC 652 is Historic.

questions: what does the telnet naocrd option do
subtitle: A Telnet option for agreeing who handles output carriage returns.

tldr.problem: Telnet peers may need to agree which side handles carriage-return characters and whether to delay, discard or otherwise treat them.
tldr.mechanism: NAOCRD uses Telnet option negotiation and an 8-bit subnegotiation value to suggest which party handles carriage returns and the disposition to use.
tldr.outcome: RFC 652 is Historic; it documents a negotiation option for carriage-return handling.

today: RFC 652 is Historic. It specifies a Telnet option for negotiating output carriage-return handling.

sections.title: Negotiating Carriage-Return Handling
sections.content:
The option is named NAOCRD, Negotiate About Output Carriage-Return Disposition, with command code 10. Telnet DO and WILL commands start or accept negotiation; DON'T and WON'T refuse it or return to the unnegotiated default. After agreement, either data sender or receiver can use an 8-bit subnegotiation value to specify which party should handle output carriage returns.

In the default state, neither side is required or prohibited from handling carriage returns, though the RFC says it is appropriate for at least the receiver to handle them primitively.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender and receiver can agree which side handles carriage returns. If they do not negotiate, neither side is required to do so, though the RFC says the receiver handling them is appropriate.

sections.title: Disposition Values
sections.content:
Value 0 says the command sender alone will handle carriage returns. Values 1–250 ask the other party to handle them with a delay measured in character-times or inserted NULs. Value 252 asks the other party to handle and discard them. Value 254 asks the other party to handle them while the sender waits for a character on the reverse simplex connection before sending more; the RFC warns that phase problems can occur. Value 255 asks the other party to handle them without specifying how. Values 251 and 253 are not allowed.

If neither party wants to handle carriage returns, the receiver must do so; if both want to, the sender handles them.
sections.plainLanguage: The value tells the peer who should handle the carriage return and may specify a delay, discarding it or no particular method. The RFC also sets rules for what happens when both or neither side wants to handle it.

sections.title: Historic Status
sections.content: RFC 652 is classified as Historic. Its text defines the NAOCRD command meanings, default state and disposition values; it does not describe later Telnet or terminal practices.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 652 is Historic. It records the rules for this Telnet option.
